title: The dart of grief
hook: life is short and uncertain; draw out the dart of lamentation

segments.voice: Yesterday: four marks of good speech, and the poet who put them in verse. Your line was true and kind. Did one true, kind sentence land? Today the Sutta Nipata turns to the hardest thing anyone says goodbye to. Day six hundred three.

There's a drawer in many homes that nobody opens much. A watch that stopped. A card in a handwriting you'd know anywhere. A phone number you can't quite bring yourself to delete. Grief has a way of lodging somewhere and staying. The eighth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter is called the Salla Sutta, the discourse on the dart. It doesn't open with comfort. It opens with the plain facts of death, and then it uses a picture every archer and every healer in ancient India would have known: something sharp, stuck in the chest, that has to come out. Today: the dart of grief.
screen: `A DRAWER NOBODY OPENS.` → `GRIEF LODGES AND STAYS.` → `THE SALLA SUTTA, SN 3.8.`

segments.voice: The verses begin bluntly. The life of mortals here is unmarked by any sign of how long it will last, short, and tied up with pain. There's no way for those born not to die. The poem then piles up images. As ripe fruit is in danger of falling early, so the born are always in danger of death. As clay pots made by a potter all end up broken, so it is with life. Young and old, foolish and wise, all go under death's power. Even as relatives look on, weeping, each one is led away. Then the turn. The wise, seeing how the world is, don't add grief on grief. Weeping and wailing, the poem says, don't bring back the one who's gone; they only harm the one who weeps, who grows thin and pale, while the dead are not helped at all. So, the poem says, draw out the dart: the dart of lamenting, of longing, of grief, and you'll find peace. Two things are worth noticing. First, the dart is in the mourner, not in the one who died. The poem isn't saying the loss doesn't matter. It's saying the wound is real and can heal. Second, Pali salla is the word for a barbed arrow or a splinter, the thing a healer pulls out. The poem is firm: lamenting helps no one. But its picture is a healer's, not a judge's. A barb is something to be drawn out with care, not something you're blamed for carrying.
screen: `NO SIGN OF HOW LONG.` · `RIPE FRUIT, CLAY POTS.` · `WEEPING DOESN'T BRING THEM BACK.` · `THE DART IS IN THE MOURNER.` · then, large: `DRAW OUT THE DART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit gently with grief. If there's someone you've lost, a person, an animal, a time of your life, let them come to mind. You don't have to do anything with the feeling. Just find where it sits in the body: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Breathe near it, the way you'd sit beside someone in a hospital bed. If nothing comes, think of someone you know who is grieving, and simply wish them ease. The bell holds the time.
Salla, a barbed dart. In the Salla Sutta, lamenting lodged in the one who mourns, a real wound, which can be drawn out. Today's word.
Your line: draw out the dart. Today, if a memory stings, don't push it away and don't press on it. Let it be there, breathe once, and notice that you're still here. Day six hundred three.

howItsDone: Verses on impermanence are often chanted at Buddhist funerals and memorial services, and in many Theravada communities monks are invited to chant and teach for the family in the days after a death.

fork.setup: someone you love has died. you've wept for days and can't eat. according to the Salla Sutta, what helps the one who has died?
options: more weeping, to show how much they mattered.
nothing in your weeping helps them; it only harms you.
fork.reveal: the poem says plainly that lamenting doesn't reach the dead and only wears down the living. so it asks the mourner to draw out the dart.

original.note: Pali salla: a dart, barbed arrow or splinter. the Salla Sutta is Sn 3.8.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says don't grieve.
what it means: the dart is real and it's in the mourner; the poem asks that it be drawn out, not denied.
what a scholar hears: salla, the barbed arrow, recurs in the early texts: the arrow of craving, the poisoned arrow of MN 63, the second arrow of SN 36.6.
recall: a sage, a silent wise one

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.8 (Salla Sutta), the dart of grief

notes: Sn 3.8 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the ripe-fruit and potter's-pot similes, the relatives looking on, and 'grows thin and pale'.
The listener is invited to grieve gently; the script avoids telling anyone to stop mourning. A Keeper may want to add how communities actually support mourners.
Earlier days touch arrows: day 74 (Kisa Gotami), 257 (the second arrow), 346 (the poisoned arrow). Today's angle is the dart lodged in the mourner.

Audit (second sample): replaced the teach's closing lines, which softened the poem ('not a command to stop feeling') and leaned on an unsourced 'many teachers describe it'; the new lines keep the poem's firmness and the healer's image.
